1.note: These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine them and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how you as a team have decided to translate the parallel phrases in the Psalms, and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Hear my prayer, Yahweh; yes, listen to my pleas]

Here, **to your face** represents being in the presence of God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in your presence]

The word translated as **for** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]

David is saying **everyone living is not righteous** as a generalization for emphasis. If it would be clearer in your language, you could express the emphasis in a different way. Alternate translation: [no living person is truly righteous]

3.note: The word translated as **For** indicates that what follows is a reason for what came before. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that what follows is a reason for what came before. Alternate translation: [This is because]
Here, **my soul** represents David himself. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [the enemy has pursued me]

Here David is speaking as if his enemy had physically **crushed** his **life to the ground**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [he has completely defeated me] or [he has brought me very low]

Here David is speaking as if his suffering were being in **dark places**. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [in places of despair] or [in places where it is as if I were dead]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the dead of ages** are unable to help themselves, so is David in his suffering. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [like people who have been dead for a long time]

David is using the adjective **dead** as a noun to mean a certain kind of person. Your language may use adjectives in the same way. If not, you can translate this adjective with an equivalent phrase. Alternate translation: [like those who died long ago]

4.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [So my spirit and my heart lose hope within me]

Here David is speaking as if his **spirit** were a person who could **faint**. He means that he is losing his strength and vitality. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am growing weak inside]

Here the **heart** represents where David’s feelings exist. He is saying that deep inside himself he feels dismay. You may have a comparable expression in your language, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I feel hopeless]

5.note: See how your translation team has decided to represent pairs of phrases in Hebrew poetry that mean basically the same thing. Alternate translation: [In my mind I review all that you have done] or [I meditate on all your works; indeed, I reflect on the works of your hands]

Here, **your hands** represents God’s power and agency. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [on what you have accomplished]

6.note: Here David is speaking as if to **spread out** his **hands** were the act of praying itself. He means that he is praying to God. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I lift my hands in prayer to you] or [I pray earnestly to you]

David is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [my soul longs for you as a weary land longs for water]

The point of this comparison is that just as **a weary land** desperately needs water, so David desperately needs God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [I need you the way a weary land needs rain]

Here David is speaking as if his **spirit** were something that could be **expiring** or used up. He means that he is losing all hope and strength. Your language may have a comparable expression that you can use in your translation, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I am losing all strength] or [I have no more endurance]

Here, **your face** represents God’s attention and favor. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [Do not hide your favor from me] or [Do not ignore me]

The word translated as **or** indicates that what follows is a negative consequence that will happen if the previous request is not fulfilled. Use a connector in your language that makes this clear. Alternate translation: [otherwise]

David is referring to death in a polite way by using the phrase **the descenders of the pit**. Depending on what is helpful for your readers, you could use a polite way of referring to this in your language, or you could state this plainly. Alternate translation: [those who descend to their death] or [those who die]
